pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 8-9. Round any number to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000 by deciding which multiple it is CLOSER to on the number line (4,367 → 4,370 / 4,400 / 4,000), using the midpoint as the tipping point and the convention 'halfway rounds up'.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 4): 'round any number to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.NBT.3 'use place-value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place'.
• Operational details — Teach rounding as a nearness decision on the number line FIRST: mark the two bounding multiples, find the midpoint, and see which side the number sits. Only then formalise the 'look at the next digit' rule, justified by the midpoint. Emphasise that the target place determines the bounding multiples, and handle the halfway convention and cascade cases (e.g. 4,970 to nearest 100). Link to estimation.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8, emerging): rounds to the nearest 10 using a number line. Tier B (age 8-9, secure): rounds to 10/100/1000 and explains via nearer multiple / midpoint. Tier C (age 9, extending): handles halfway and cascade cases and uses rounding to estimate calculations.
bestPractices: Teach rounding as a nearness decision on the number line before any digit rule — the line gives the meaning.
Always mark the two bounding multiples and the midpoint; the midpoint is the tipping point.
Derive the 'look at the next digit' rule FROM the midpoint so it is understood, not memorised.
Make explicit that the target place chooses the bounding multiples (nearest 100 → bound by hundreds).
Teach the halfway-rounds-up convention and cascade cases (4,970 → 5,000 to nearest 100) deliberately; link to estimating calculations.
keyRepresentations: Number line with the two bounding multiples and midpoint (the canonical model)
Place-value chart to identify the rounding digit and the decider digit
commonMisconceptions: Rounding by the wrong digit or to the wrong place (ignoring which place is the target).
Always rounding down (truncating) or always up.
Chained/successive rounding (rounding the ones then tens then…) instead of one decision.
Mishandling the halfway case or the cascade (4,970 to nearest 100 → 4,900 not 5,000).
Treating rounding as a rule with no sense of 'nearer to', so unable to check reasonableness.

learn.summary: For ages 8-9: round whole numbers to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000 by treating rounding as a nearness decision on a number line FIRST — mark the two bounding multiples, find the midpoint, and see which side the number sits — then formalise the 'look at the next digit' rule as a shortcut justified by the midpoint. Core worked example: 4,367 rounds to 4,370 (nearest 10), 4,400 (nearest 100), 4,000 (nearest 1000). Deliberately teach the halfway convention (half rounds up) and cascade/carry cases (4,970 → 5,000 to nearest 100). Includes a number-line manipulation activity, a consolidation assessment with targeted traps, and a static reference image as a scaffold.

activities.title: Number-line rounding bench: snap to the nearer multiple
feedback: If a learner rounds 4,367 to 4,300, drag the marker and point to the midpoint 4,350: 4,367 is past it, so it is nearer 4,400.

If a learner uses the wrong digit for nearest 100 (inspecting the 7, which is the ones digit, or the 3, the hundreds digit itself, instead of the 6, the tens digit that decides), name the decider digit — one place to the right of the rounding place — mark it, and look only at that.
If a learner keeps trailing digits (4,367 → 4,467, or keeps the 67), show on the line that the rounded value must be a multiple of 100, so everything after the hundreds becomes zero.
For the cascade 4,970 → 5,000, walk the single carry rather than reteaching everything: 4,970 is 49 hundreds and 70, so 49 hundreds + 1 = 50 hundreds = 5,000; rehearse near the boundary.
activities.rationale: Grounding rounding in number-line nearness and the midpoint before formalising the digit rule builds understanding and helps avoid rote truncation errors; dragging across the midpoint makes the decision rule concrete and visible. The place selector and cascade animation are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism tangible, not mandatory implementation.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'round any number to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000'.
Use place-value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place (4.NBT.3).
Rounding should be grounded in number-line nearness and the midpoint before the digit rule is formalised, to avoid rote truncation errors.
learnerActions: Place or drag the target number (e.g. 4,367) as a marker on a number line between its two bounding multiples — 4,300 and 4,400 when rounding to the nearest 100 — with the midpoint 4,350 clearly flagged.
See that 4,367 sits PAST the midpoint, so it is nearer to 4,400; watch the marker snap to 4,400 (an arc or snap animation makes the 'nearer multiple' choice visible rather than recited).

Drag the marker back and forth across the midpoint and watch the rounded result flip at 4,350: whole numbers below 4,350 (e.g. 4,349) round down to 4,300, while 4,350 itself and anything above round up to 4,400. This shows that the midpoint is the tipping point, and that the half-rounds-up convention decides the exact-halfway case.
Use a target-place selector (10/100/1000) that rescales the line and changes the bounding multiples, so you feel how the target place chooses which multiples bound the number.
Work a cascade case: round 4,970 to the nearest 100 and watch the roll up to 5,000 — the hundreds carry over (49 hundreds + 1 = 50 hundreds = 5,000).
After the line meaning is built, name the 'decider' digit — the one immediately to the right of the place you are rounding to — and connect it to which side of the midpoint you are on.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding means choosing the nearer multiple of the target place; the midpoint is the tipping point, and the 'look at the next digit' rule is just a quick way of telling whether the number is below halfway (decider 0-4, round down) or at or past halfway (decider 5-9, round up, with exactly halfway going up by the agreed convention).

activities.title: Consolidation across places with targeted traps
feedback: For a halfway case like 2,650 to the nearest 100, if the learner always rounds down (2,600), state the agreed convention (half rounds up, so 2,650 → 2,700) and mark the midpoint on the line so they see 2,650 is exactly halfway and the rule decides.
For 1,970 to the nearest 100, the carried answer is 2,000; if they produce 1,900 or a malformed value, walk the single carry: 1,970 is 19 hundreds and 70, so 19 hundreds + 1 = 20 hundreds = 2,000.
If a rounded answer is not a clean multiple of the target place, return to the number line to show the rounded value must land exactly on a multiple.
activities.rationale: After the line meaning is built, varied practice across places with specific traps consolidates the procedure and surfaces the remaining failure mechanisms (wrong decider digit, halfway habit, carry past 9). A recognition/fill format is useful for consolidation and checking; note it does not by itself elicit independent construction of the number-line justification, which the first activity provides.
sourceClaims: Year 4 pupils should 'round any number to the nearest 10, 100 or 1000'.
Use place-value understanding to round multi-digit whole numbers to any place (4.NBT.3).
learnerActions: Round given numbers to the nearest 10, 100 and 1000 (e.g. round 4,367 to each place) via fill-in or multiple choice.
First select the target place, then round, so the two steps stay distinct.
Tackle deliberately chosen trap cases: the halfway case 2,650 to the nearest 100 (which rounds up to 2,700), and the cascade case 1,970 to the nearest 100 (which carries to 2,000).
Match numbers to their rounded values across places.
activities.intendedInsight: Rounding can be applied reliably across different target places, including the halfway (5) and nine-cascade cases, once the nearness meaning is secure.

activities.title: Rounding-hill reference image (scaffold)
feedback: If a learner cannot say why a number rounds a certain way, point to the midpoint on the hill and ask which side the number is on.
Prompt the learner to then carry out the nearness decision themselves on a live number line, not just read it off the poster.
activities.rationale: A static image or 'roll to nearer multiple' tap is a helpful reference and reminder, but the nearness decision is best made by the learner acting on a line; treat this as a scaffold that supports, rather than replaces, active rounding.
sourceClaims: Rounding should be grounded in number-line nearness and the midpoint before the digit rule is formalised, to avoid rote truncation errors.
learnerActions: Use a static rounding-hill / number-line poster showing the two bounding multiples and the marked midpoint as a reference while rounding.
Optionally tap a number on the hill to watch it roll to the nearer multiple, with the midpoint marked, as a reminder of the nearness decision.
activities.intendedInsight: A visual 'hill' with a marked midpoint reminds learners that rounding goes to the nearer multiple and that the midpoint decides direction.

constraints: Teach rounding as a number-line nearness decision FIRST; only then formalise the 'look at the next digit' rule, justified by the midpoint, so it is understood rather than memorised.
Always mark the two bounding multiples and the midpoint; the target place chooses the bounding multiples (nearest 100 → bound by hundreds).

Deliberately teach the halfway-rounds-up convention and cascade/carry cases (e.g. 4,970 → 5,000 to nearest 100); state the convention explicitly since 'half rounds up' is a chosen convention, not a mathematical necessity.
The rounded value must be a multiple of the target place: all digits after the rounding place become zero.
Avoid chained/successive rounding (rounding ones, then tens, then hundreds); rounding to a target place is a single decision from the original number.

The static hill/poster is a reference scaffold; its limit is that it shows rather than requires the learner's own nearness decision. A fill/multiple-choice format consolidates and checks but does not by itself require the learner to construct the number-line justification.
When assessing, watch the working (which digit decides and what happens to trailing digits), not only the final number, to reveal which rule the child is running.

The decider digit for a target place is the digit one place to the RIGHT of it (for 4,367 to nearest 100 the decider is the tens digit 6, not the hundreds digit 3, the ones digit 7, or the thousands digit 4).
Carry arithmetic must match the actual number: 4,970 → 49 hundreds + 1 = 50 hundreds = 5,000; 1,970 → 19 hundreds + 1 = 20 hundreds = 2,000.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The candidate originally miscomputed the 4,970 cascade carry as '19 hundreds + 1 = 20 hundreds = 2,000' (reasoning that belongs to 1,970). Corrected to 49 hundreds + 1 = 50 hundreds = 5,000 at every learner-facing occurrence.

The source's wrong-decider-digit misconception listed 'the 7 or the 4' for 4,367 to the nearest hundred; the 4 is the thousands digit and contradicts the pattern's own description (hundreds digit itself or ones digit). Corrected to the 7 (ones) or the 3 (hundreds digit itself), with 6 (tens) as the correct decider.

The source assessment includes a double-rounding probe (4,347): rounding to the nearest ten gives 4,350, then to the nearest hundred (half-up) gives 4,400, whereas rounding straight to the nearest hundred gives 4,300 — these differ. Any demonstration must make clear the straight-to-hundred answer (4,300) is correct and chained rounding is the error being exposed.

The source correctAnswer '4,400; 2,000; 2,700' maps to the diagnosticPrompt cases (4,367 / 1,970 / 2,650 to nearest hundred), not the probeDeeper prompts (e.g. 2,999 to nearest ten is 3,000); these probe numbers were not reconstructable and were not propagated into learner-facing material. Reviewers should confirm intended probe numbers and answers.

The original row's '3D adds nothing' / 'open dialogue adds little' fit judgements were catalog preferences and are not propagated as universal claims. A number line is naturally planar, but this does not establish that other media cannot support rounding.

Two of three sources are marked unverified in the source row; comparative efficacy or necessity of the number-line-first approach is not independently established here beyond the cited claim about grounding rounding in nearness.

probeDeeper: Round 2,999 to the nearest ten — what happens to the other digits?
Show me on a number line why 4,367 rounds to 4,400 and not 4,300.
Round 4,347 to the nearest ten, then round THAT to the nearest hundred. Now round 4,347 straight to the nearest hundred — do you get the same? (double-rounding)
assess.correctAnswer: 4,400; 2,000; 2,700 — deciding by the digit one place to the right of the hundreds, then replacing all digits after the hundreds place with zero.

errorPatterns.pattern: Decides using the wrong digit — the hundreds digit itself, or the final (ones) digit — instead of the digit one place to the right of the rounding place
errorPatterns.nextMove: Name the 'decider' digit: the one immediately to the right of the place you're rounding to. Mark it, then look only at that. Reground with place-value columns.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For 4,367 to the nearest hundred the child inspects the 7 or the 4, not the 6.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rounds the target digit but leaves the trailing digits unchanged (4,367 → 4,467, or keeps the 67)
errorPatterns.nextMove: On a number line, show the rounded value must be a multiple of 100 — so everything after the hundreds becomes zero.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The rounded answer still carries the original tens/ones.

errorPatterns.pattern: Always rounds a 5 down (or always up) regardless of convention: 2,650 → 2,600
errorPatterns.nextMove: State the class convention (half rounds up) and mark the midpoint on a number line so they see 2,650 is exactly halfway and the rule decides.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Halfway case is resolved by a fixed 'down' habit rather than the agreed rule.

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to carry when rounding up past a 9: 1,970 → 1,900 or 1,1000 instead of 2,000
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't reteach the whole procedure — walk the single carry: 19 hundreds + 1 = 20 hundreds = 2,000. Rehearse on a number line near the boundary.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The nine-cascade case gives a malformed or non-carried answer.

responseLevels.gap: Uses the wrong decider digit or leaves trailing digits in place; rounded value is not a clean multiple.
responseLevels.full: Rounds to nearest 10/100/1000 accurately including the 5 and 9-cascade cases, zeroes trailing digits, and justifies by nearer multiple on a number line.
responseLevels.partial: Rounds clear cases correctly but mishandles the halfway 5, the carry past 9, or which place to look at.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set the task and watch the working: 'Round 4,367 to the nearest hundred. Now round 1,970 to the nearest hundred. Now round 2,650 to the nearest hundred.' Ask them to show it on a number line for at least one. Watch which digit they use to decide and what they do to the digits after it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The three cases are chosen to trip specific mechanisms: 4,367 checks whether trailing digits are zeroed; 1,970 forces a carry past 9 into the thousands; 2,650 is the halfway (5) case. Watching the working — not the final number alone — reveals which rule the child is running.
